extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP counsel, patent prosecutors and litigators, in-house counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the USPTO's proposed rule requiring terminal disclaimers to contain enforceability conditions linking enforceability to whether the patent is directly or indirectly tied to a patent with a claim finally held invalid; discusses definitions, examples, scope, and practical prosecution and litigation implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed terminal-disclaimer enforceability clause
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO proposes requiring any terminal disclaimer to include a clause stipulating that a terminally disclaimed patent will be enforceable only if the patent is not and has never been tied directly or indirectly to a patent in which any claim has been finally held invalid as anticipated or obvious in a civil litigation or a USPTO proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposed clause would be in addition to the current requirements that a terminal disclaimer tie the expiration and ownership of patents. The rule would apply across industries and at all stages of product development; it is not limited to Hatch-Waxman or BPCIA contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of applicability (all patents, all stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule applies to all patents and at all stages of product development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although motivated by concerns about drug-cost policy and Hatch-Waxman/BPCIA contexts, the USPTO explicitly extends the requirement beyond those statutes to any industry with long product development cycles or multiple patented inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'directly' tied via terminal disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is 'directly' tied by a terminal disclaimer to 'another patent' when: (1) the terminal disclaimer is filed in the subject patent or application; and (2) the other patent, or the application that issued as the other patent, is the reference patent or application identified in the terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two patents are directly tied, only one terminal disclaimer is at issue. Under the proposed rule, a direct tie can render the subject patent unenforceable if a claim of the reference patent is finally held unpatentable or invalid and the terminal disclaimer contains the proposed agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'indirectly' tied via terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is 'indirectly' tied by two terminal disclaimers to 'another patent' when: (1) a terminal disclaimer filed in the subject patent or application identifies an intermediate patent/application as the reference patent or application; and (2) a terminal disclaimer filed in the intermediate patent/application identifies the other patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect tying can involve chains of two or more terminal disclaimers (e.g., W ← X ← Y). The USPTO's examples (Examples 2–5) show how enforcement consequences can cascade along such chains if the proposed agreement is present in the terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unidirectionality of tying
rubrics_metrics.description: "Tying by a terminal disclaimer is unidirectional and is effective only for the patent with the terminal disclaimer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tying is unidirectional, relationships like X → Y ← Z can produce asymmetric consequences: X and Z may both be tied to Y, but X and Z are not tied to each other. The proposed enforceability condition only operates in the direction of the terminal disclaimer(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceability consequence when a tied patent has a claim finally held invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim of a referenced patent is finally held unpatentable or invalid over prior art, patents tied (directly or indirectly, as defined) to that referenced patent may not be enforceable if their terminal disclaimers contain the proposed agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Register examples demonstrate specific chain outcomes: e.g., in W ← X ← Y ← Z, if a claim of W is held invalid and the terminal disclaimer in Z contains the proposed agreement, Z may not be enforced. These consequences depend on the presence of the proposed enforceability clause in the terminal disclaimers in the chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory presumption of validity (35 U.S.C. § 282) and terminal disclaimer effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 282, 'Each claim of a patent ... shall be presumed valid independently of the validity of other claims; dependent or multiple dependent claims shall be presumed valid even though dependent upon an invalid claim.' Historically, filing a terminal disclaimer is not an admission of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule would require a patent owner filing a terminal disclaimer to abandon part of that statutory presumption of validity and to give up the current legal presumption that filing a terminal disclaimer is not an admission of obviousness (citing Motionless Keyboard Co. v. Microsoft Corp. and Quad Environmental Techs. Corp. v. Union Sanitary Dist.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that valid, nonobvious claims become unenforceable due to ties
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent containing nonobvious (patentable distinct) claims may become unenforceable simply because it is directly or indirectly tied via terminal disclaimers to a patent that contains a single claim found anticipated or obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative prosecution scenarios: (a) A genus claim directly tied to a species claim can make the species claim unenforceable if the genus has a claim later held invalid. (b) Chains of continuation/species filings can lead to an indirectly tied species becoming unenforceable even if its claims are patentably distinct from upstream claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical prosecution strategy impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed rule is implemented, applicants will need to change prosecution strategies to avoid unintentionally creating unenforceable patents via terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential adaptations include: prosecuting broader claim sets early to provoke a restriction requirement (which may be uneconomic due to excess claim fees); spending time and resources to traverse obviousness-type double patenting rejections rather than filing terminal disclaimers; expecting additional rounds of arguments and appeals, higher prosecution costs, and delays in grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO policy rationale for the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO states the rule 'is intended to promote competition by lowering the cost of challenging groups of patents tied by terminal disclaimers, resulting in reduced barriers to market entry and lower costs for consumers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO also asserts that narrowing validity disputes to only one patent tied by terminal disclaimers could lead to more focused claim construction hearings, lower litigation costs, and faster resolution, and allow only one patent to be challenged via post-grant challenge. The article notes the USPTO provided no empirical evidence in the Federal Register notice to support the proposition that the rule will reduce prices for consumers.
